chief_complaint: unintended weight loss, difficulty swallowing solid foods, and fatigue
hpi_details: A 64-year-old female presents to the clinic with unintended weight loss, progressive difficulty swallowing solid foods, and fatigue. She reports a 15-year history of poorly-controlled gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and continues to smoke about 10 cigarettes a day. Symptoms have been gradually worsening over the past two months.
ideas: She thinks years of severe stomach acid splashing up into her throat have created tight scar tissue that is narrowing her food pipe.
concerns: She is worried that her smoking and chronic heartburn have turned into a malignant tumor like her brother had, meaning she won't be able to eat solid food again.
expectations: She hopes to be referred for a camera test down her throat and to get urgent advice on foods or liquid supplements she can swallow safely.
pmh: 15-year history of chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD), obesity

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Oesophageal Adenocarcinoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes ordering an urgent upper endoscopy (EGD) with biopsy and a chest/abdominal CT scan, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Oesophageal Adenocarcinoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Peptic stricture (benign) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Progressive dysphagia with unintentional weight loss — a combination that always needs urgent endoscopy.
management_principles: Order urgent upper endoscopy (EGD) with biopsy, chest/abdominal CT scan
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 64F with a 15-year history of poorly-controlled GERD and ongoing smoking presents with progressive dysphagia to solids, unintentional weight loss, and fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Esophageal Adenocarcinoma.
reference_soap.assessment: Oesophageal adenocarcinoma arising in the setting of long-standing GERD. DDx: peptic stricture (benign), achalasia, severe GERD without malignancy.
reference_soap.plan: Order urgent upper endoscopy (EGD) with biopsy, chest/abdominal CT scan. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Esophageal Adenocarcinoma
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Esophageal Adenocarcinoma
Implement evidence-based management plan: Order urgent upper endoscopy (EGD) with biopsy, chest/abdominal CT scan

teaching.one_liner: A tumour in the lower oesophagus, often arising from long-standing acid reflux, progressively narrows the passage so solid food sticks and weight falls off.
red_flags: Progressive dysphagia with unintentional weight loss — a combination that always needs urgent endoscopy

must_ask.say: Has the swallowing difficulty been getting worse, moving from solids toward liquids too?
Have you had heartburn or acid reflux for many years before this started?
How much weight have you lost, and how quickly?
Do you smoke, or have you smoked in the past?
Does it hurt when you swallow, or just feel stuck?
Do you ever bring food back up after eating?

history.answer: I've lost a lot of weight without trying over the last couple of months, and lately food keeps getting stuck in my chest when I swallow.
I've lost about six kilograms over the past two months. My clothes have become noticeably looser on me.
No, I haven't been dieting or exercising to lose weight at all. It just came off on its own.
My appetite is a bit lower, but mainly I've been eating much less because it feels so uncomfortable when food gets stuck.
It started about two months ago with meat and crusty bread getting stuck behind my breastbone, and now even softer foods hesitate on the way down. Liquids still go down without trouble.
Yes, I feel a dull, aching pain behind my breastbone right as the food tries to pass through.
I've had severe burning in my chest and sour fluid backing up into my throat for about fifteen years, especially when lying down.
Sometimes chunks of food come right back up into my mouth after I try to swallow, but I don't have constant nausea or vomiting.
My bowel movements are regular once a day. I haven't noticed any black tarry stools or red blood.
No, I haven't had any diarrhea, and my stool doesn't look greasy or float.
No racing heartbeat, and I haven't had tremors or trouble tolerating warm rooms.
No, I'm not unusually thirsty, and I'm not waking up at night to urinate.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
I don't have a cough, and I have never coughed up any phlegm or blood.
No, I haven't felt any lumps in my neck, underarms, or groin.
I feel quite worn out and worried about what might be wrong, but I haven't been feeling depressed.
My brother passed away from throat cancer a few years ago, and with my smoking, I'm terrified that this food sticking in my chest is a tumor.
I live with my husband and have no trouble cooking or buying food, and my teeth are in good shape.
I had an endoscopy about five years ago for my reflux and was told my esophagus was very irritated, but I never went back for follow-up.
No, I've never had tuberculosis and have never been around anyone with it.

I thought years of stomach acid splashing up into my throat might have just caused bad scar tissue that's tightening up my throat. My brother passed away from throat cancer a few years ago, and with my smoking, I'm terrified that this food sticking in my chest is a tumor.
Aside from chronic acid reflux disease for fifteen years and being told I am overweight, I haven't had other major illnesses.
I had my appendix removed when I was twenty-two, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I have a prescription for omeprazole twenty milligrams once a day, but I often forget to take it unless the burning is unbearable.
I don't have any known allergies to medicines or food.
I've smoked about half a pack of cigarettes a day for forty years, so about twenty pack-years.
I only have a glass of wine or beer on special social occasions, maybe once or twice a month.
I'm retired from retail work and live quietly with my husband.
My father died of a heart attack in his late seventies and my mother had high blood pressure, but there is no family history of cancer.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Overweight female who appears mildly fatigued but in no acute cardiopulmonary distress.
Mild conjunctival pallor noted bilaterally; sclerae are anicteric.
Oral mucosa is moist without ulcerations or visible pharyngeal masses; dentition is intact.
No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy; Virchow node is absent.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, and non-tender without palpable nodules.
Breath sounds are clear to auscultation bilaterally without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds and no audible murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is obese, soft, with mild tenderness to deep palpation in the epigastrium, but without guarding or rebound tenderness.
No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly appreciated; no palpable abdominal masses.
Normal perianal inspection; normal sphincter tone with no rectal masses palpable, and brown stool on glove without gross blood.
No pitting edema or calf swelling in either lower extremity.
